results.message: Explain identify the material with an example.
results.answer: To identify a material, look at what each part of the item is actually made from. Do not rely only on its colour, appearance, picture, recycling triangle or plastic code. For example, a snack package may have a cardboard sleeve and a soft-plastic wrapper, so identify and check each part separately. A scrunchable film is soft plastic, while plain cardboard is paper-based material. Then check the instructions and your local collection service, because acceptance varies by council.

results.message: Explain notice avoidable waste with an example.
results.answer: Noticeable food waste is food that is thrown away because it was forgotten or overlooked, rather than used. For example, checking your kitchen before shopping might reveal a carrot that could be added to your next meal instead of being left unused. This is an observation—not a measurement of your personal waste.

results.message: Explain connect waste and climate with an example.
results.answer: Food waste connects to climate because food uses land, water and energy before it is eaten. When edible food is discarded, those resources have been used without providing a meal. Globally, food loss and waste together are linked to 8–10% of annual greenhouse-gas emissions; this is not a measure of one person’s emissions savings. Example: plan portions and store leftovers so they are eaten, while putting unavoidable scraps in an accepted organics collection where available. SDG 13.3 supports learning and awareness about these climate connections.

results.message: Explain plan with available food with an example.
results.answer: Start before shopping by checking your fridge, freezer and pantry. Choose food that needs using soon and is still safe, then plan a meal around it. Plan for the people who will eat, link meals that share ingredients, and add only missing items to your list. For example, if you have carrots and half a tub of an ingredient, plan a meal using them before buying more. If plans change, review perishables and make a safe storage plan.

results.message: Explain put safety first with an example.
results.answer: Put safety first by following the food’s label, storage instructions and date limits. A use-by date is a safety limit: do not eat the food after it. For example, keep perishable food refrigerated at 5°C or colder, and plan to use it before its use-by date. A best-before date mainly concerns quality, but storage and condition still matter.

results.message: Explain prevent surplus first with an example.
results.answer: Prevent surplus first by checking what you already have before shopping and planning around food that needs using soon, while keeping it safe. Plan for the people who will eat and buy only what is missing; a larger bargain is not helpful if you cannot use it. Example: use your carrots and half a tub of an ingredient to plan a meal, then add only missing items to your shopping list. If plans change, review perishables and make a safe storage plan.

results.message: 请简单解释先预防多余食物。
results.answer:
先预防多余食物，就是在购物前先查看冰箱、冷冻室和储物柜，优先安排使用仍安全、需要尽快吃的食物；再根据实际人数和份量购物，只购买缺少的东西。这样能减少食物被遗忘或买得过多，也能避免浪费生产食物所需的土地、水和能源。

例子：如果家里有胡萝卜和半盒食材，就先用它们计划一餐，再列出缺少的物品，而不是马上买一套新食材。

results.message: Explain read dates and scope with an example.
results.answer: Check both the source’s publication date and its scope. For example, the UNFCCC article was published on 30 September 2024 and reports that food loss and food waste together are linked to 8–10% of annual global greenhouse-gas emissions. “Global” means worldwide, not your household or a measurement of emissions saved by this learner. An everyday example: saying “the 2024 global estimate includes both food lost before sale and food wasted later” is more accurate than saying “my actions saved 8–10%.”
